1:
On the soft answer all agree; the interest is in how they enforce it. Delitzsch points out that the two words for anger are chosen deliberately, the second the ordinary term drawn from breathing through the nostrils, the first the word for anger at its hottest, from a root meaning to glow; a mild word turns that heat back. He caps it with a Latin jingle: heavy anger breaks when the reply is sweet. Gill supplies the meteorology, high winds being laid by soft showers, and he and Henry both cite a tribe pacified by a general's mild reply. Henry adds the counter-case, the same tribe exasperated later by a rougher man with worse consequences, and draws the rule that hard arguments do best with soft words. Clarke states the mechanism: one angry word begets another, the temper of one spirit reproducing itself in another, so gentleness disarms all but the mad.

The tongue that uses knowledge aright is defined by what it avoids. Delitzsch reads the Hebrew idiom as doing a thing in a masterly way, as one strikes a harp well, so the wise tongue brings great knowledge to light; the Greek, he notes, read a different word in the second clause, and one modern scholar prefers it. Ellicott and Wesley make the point timing and manner. Clarke makes the difficulty explicit: when to speak and when to be silent, what to say and what to leave unsaid, what manner suits the occasion and the persons — all hard even for wise men, since wise counsel may still be foolishly given. Henry adds that to a man who both has knowledge and uses it well, more will be given. On the seventh verse Henry adds the complementary duty: knowledge is used rightly only when dispersed, so it is a fault to pour out folly and a shame not to scatter what one knows.

The omnipresent eye is the group's theological centre, and they divide over its tone. Henry treats it as doctrine enforcing morality, and gives it his best sentence: angels are full of eyes, but God is all eye. He takes the verse for providence as much as omniscience, secret sins, services and sorrows all under inspection. Clarke separates the two effects. That the divine eye is everywhere is calculated to appal a man whose heart is not right and who wants privacy for his wickedness; that the divine providence is everywhere is calculated to encourage the upright in danger. Ellicott turns the watching into two waits, one until an iniquity is full, one for a chance to help. Delitzsch keeps to the verb, glossed as observing and holding fast: men are examined whether good or evil and kept so close that nothing escapes.

The healing tongue draws the first real disagreement, over whose spirit the perverse tongue breaks. Ellicott says another's, glossing the perverseness as distortion of the truth. Wesley and Henry say both, the speaker wounded in conscience while the hearer is left with guilt or grief. Delitzsch declines a rendering that makes the fault violence — asperity, as though violent speech were a stormy sea — and takes it for perversity, the opposite of truthfulness and kindness; gentleness, on his account, marks a tongue that delivers instruction, correction or consolation without rudeness. Clarke notices only that the figure alludes to the tree of the garden. Two smaller points close the tile. Delitzsch prefers to read the fifth verse as saying the man who regards reproof is prudent rather than that he acts prudently, conceding that the contrast favours the other. On the treasure of the righteous he argues that the Hebrew noun means not force but store, connecting it with a verb for laying up in granaries; Henry holds that religion makes men diligent and just and so increases an estate, but that the blessing on a just man's house makes rich without trouble.
8:
The pairing of sacrifice with prayer is taken as deliberate. Delitzsch observes that the same could be said of a godless man's prayer and an upright man's sacrifice, yet the assignment is not accidental: sacrifice, a material performance required by law, stands nearer to dead works than prayer, which completes itself in a word. Wesley makes the contrast one of cost, the most expensive service against the cheapest. Ellicott draws the moral: men assume that what costs trouble and expense must please God, even when the one thing he cares for is missing. Clarke agrees that no quantity of observance substitutes for holiness, and asks who counts as upright, answering that it covers the man still weary of his sin and wanting salvation as well as the man already saved. Henry supplies the motive — such sacrifices stop the mouth of conscience and keep up a reputation, as a criminal takes refuge in a sanctuary not because it is holy but because it shelters him.

The verse about correction is read three ways. The English has it grievous to the man who leaves the road. Ellicott repunctuates so that a grievous correction awaits him, first as discipline and then, if reproof is still hated, as death. Delitzsch reaches nearly the same place: whoever will not welcome instruction must receive it at last against his will as peremptory punishment, the sharp correction being the death he falls under. Gill records a third possibility, that the man has had bad discipline — due care was never taken of him, and he was neither properly taught nor corrected in season. Henry stays with conduct: of all sinners, apostates resent reproof worst.

On the unseen world the interest is lexical. Ellicott derives the first noun from a verb meaning to ask, the underworld being so named because it always asks for more and is never satisfied, and takes the second for the lowest region, the abode of evil spirits and the lost. Clarke divides them the same way, one the invisible world where separate spirits await the resurrection, the other the place of torment. Gill turns to the grave and the certainty that God knows where every man's dust lies; Henry says it better, that God needs no inscription to tell him where a man is buried. Delitzsch alone attends to the argument's form, an inference from lesser to greater, and gives its rabbinic name.

The last three are read for their psychology. On the scorner Delitzsch takes the standing contrast between mocker and wise for evidence that scepticism gained ground in Israel alongside the pursuit of wisdom, the rejection of God in principle and practice being already marked in David's time. Gill and Henry prefer a rendering that turns the aversion inward: he does not love to reprove himself and will not retire into his own heart to reason there — and Henry adds that a man's case is sad when he fears to argue with himself. On the cheerful heart Delitzsch notes only that face and spiritual habit alike follow the state within. Henry recommends harmless mirth as good for health and conversation, calls a cheerful spirit under grace an ornament to religion, and warns against melancholy as an enemy to devotion. Clarke turns physician: every sorrow works death but the sort that comes of true repentance, and a habit of sighing shortens life, each sigh throwing off some vital energy. The tile closes on two men, one who cannot get enough knowledge and one content with folly. Henry gives the first a line — if you say I have enough, you are undone — and Wesley the second, that wickedness is meat and drink to such men. Delitzsch adds that Luther read the verb as governing, where the sense is being anxiously occupied with a thing, and that the alternative Hebrew reading several scholars prefer cannot be translated at all.
15:
Who is the afflicted man of the fifteenth verse? Ellicott says he is not one weighed down by real misfortune but one who makes the worst of everything, and reads the proverb as a caution against anxiety. Delitzsch takes him for a man genuinely pressed, from without or within, and adds what decides it for him: such a man may be surrounded by any number of blessings and still find each day sad, because every morning renews the feeling of his trouble. Wesley reads the troubled in mind, Gill the poor in purse or in knowledge. Henry declines the diagnosis and turns to duty: such men are not to be censured but pitied, prayed for and relieved, since it might have been our own case, and may be yet, however merry we are now.

The two proverbs of preference are handled concretely. On the little with the fear of God, Delitzsch fixes on the noun for trouble, elsewhere used of wild confusion, making it the restless covetous care of a man enslaved to money, against the quietness that comes of fearing God. Wesley itemises tumultuous passions, vexatious cares and horrors of conscience; Clarke notes that where the fear of God is there is contentment. Henry links back to the cheerful heart of the verse before and names what produces it, holiness and love. On the dinner of herbs Gill recovers a Latin dramatist's phrase for a harsh and earthly supper, made of what grows out of the ground, cheap and quickly cooked, and notes that the Hebrew word means a traveller's meal.

The wrathful man and the sluggard draw the moralists. Henry calls passion the great make-bate, whence come wars and fightings, and observes that a quarrel carried too far breeds another; meekness he calls the peace-maker, since a man slow to anger not only prevents strife but quenches it once lit. On the sluggard's hedge all agree the thorns are imaginary. Clarke has him imagining ten thousand insuperable difficulties, every one a creature of an imagination formed by his own sloth; Henry has him pretending his way is hedged up, as though God were a hard master reaping where he had not sown; Ellicott makes each difficulty an excuse for inaction. Delitzsch worries about the wording, rejecting a proposal to emend the slothful into the tyrannical, since the contrast is not a contradiction: the sluggard is precisely a man who fails the duty of labour common to all and proper to his own calling.

Delitzsch alone reads the twentieth verse structurally: the collection opened with a proverb on honouring parents, a second main division began the same way, and the editor marks a third here with a proverb of the same kind. Henry keeps to the sentiment: the foolish son despises the mother who had most sorrow with him. On folly as a man's joy he is sharpest: the wicked man has an appetite for the bait, swallows it greedily, dreads no hook and feels none once it is down, sinning not merely without regret but with delight. Gill adds that such a man boasts of it and takes pleasure in others who do the same; Ellicott finds the folly in wasted opportunities. The last verse divides on a word. Gill records a rendering in which the missing thing is not counsel but secrecy, so a man who publishes his intentions can expect them frustrated, and Clarke suggests the plural of the second line may mean a chief of the council rather than a multitude of counsellors. Delitzsch grants that proverbs run the other way too — so many heads, so many minds — but insists no maxim against taking advice can become a rule of morals, while the rule against stubbornly following one's own head remains one. Henry puts it practically: the man who scorns to consult is defeated by circumstances a little consultation might have foreseen.
23:
Delitzsch guards the first verse against a misreading. Rendered simply as an answer, the line sounds like praise of self-satisfaction; but the Hebrew means a fitting reply, one that corresponds to what was said, so the joy is that of having hit the nail on the head — and deserved, since a reply does not always succeed. Henry makes the point from the other side: many a good word fails of the good it might have done for want of being well timed, and nothing so adorns discourse as the apt answer ready when it is wanted. Ellicott adds why such success is worth rejoicing over: the tongue does so much mischief and slips so often that a suitable reply may fairly be counted a gift of God. Gill and Wesley keep to the pleasure of being useful to a friend.

Over the upward way of life they divide about how much is being claimed. Clarke finds a threefold antithesis — the wise against the fool, above against below, life against death. Wesley makes it a matter of where a man puts his heart and treasure, Henry of escaping the snares and temptations as well as the pains of hell. Ellicott is cooler: the phrase sounds like a faint echo of the apostle's language about a citizenship above, but the writer may have meant no more than that the wise man is rewarded with long life and escapes an early death. Delitzsch notes that the way of life is one though it comprises many paths, and that the word for upwards is the one used in the earlier unresolved question whether a man's spirit rises at death.

The proud house and the widow's landmark are read as a single act of justice. Ellicott sets the two against each other — men trusting their own strength against a woman with nobody to appeal to but God — and infers from the repeated legislation against moving a boundary stone that the offence was a common form of oppression. Delitzsch identifies what is at stake as the land-possession of widows, encroached on by the proud, and defends a shortened verb form as elevated style rather than an error. Henry supplies the rule that God delights to abase the elevated and support the dejected, pride having been the ruin of multitudes; Clarke observes that such families are seldom long continued, and Wesley glosses the border as the estate within it.

On the thoughts of the wicked the English and the commentators part company. Ellicott renders the first clause thoughts of evil rather than the thoughts of evil men, and reverses the second: instead of the words of the pure being pleasant, pleasant words are pure in God's sight, accepted as coming from a well-meaning heart. Delitzsch reaches the same construction, taking the adjective neutrally: what is abominable is a bad disposition and design against others. Gill notes the same alternative and observes that even a good man has evil thoughts, abominable to himself. Henry declines to separate the halves at all, since thoughts are words to God and words are judged by the thoughts they come from. The chapter's greedy man closes the group. Ellicott identifies the gain as ill-gotten and the gifts as a judge's bribes, the word for trouble being the one applied to Achan; Delitzsch renders the first clause as doing service to avarice, and notes that from this point the Greek version mingles these proverbs with those of the next chapter. Henry describes the man himself, rising early and sitting up late, fretting at every loss and quarrelling with whoever stands in his profit's way, so becoming a vexation to his own children and servants — a portrait Gill sharpens with servants denied time to eat and sleep.
28:
The studied answer is agreed on; its text is not. Delitzsch lists what the versions made of the crucial word: the Greek read faithfulness, the Latin wrongly gave obedience from a root meaning to bow oneself, and a rabbinic reading found wormwood there, so that the righteous heart turns over the bitterness of this life. Clarke states the sense plainly — such a man's tongue never runs before his wit, since he ponders thoughts and words alike — and Wesley draws the contrast: the wicked man speaks from the mouth, not the heart, without conscience. Henry makes the governed tongue the proof that a good man is wise, and observes that it is the heart which answers, so the man says what he thinks. Gill enters a qualification: our Lord told his disciples not to premeditate a defence before persecutors, but that was an extraordinary case, and the proverb holds for ordinary ones.

The distance between God and the wicked is defined with care. Gill separates the senses at once: as to essence and power God is everywhere, and only his favour is withdrawn. Delitzsch cites an older commentator to the same effect, that the distance is not of space but of disposition, and puts it more exactly: God has withdrawn his gracious presence, so that when such men pray the prayer does not reach him. Henry supplies the reciprocity — men who tell the Almighty to depart find that he has — and Ellicott the reason the other half holds, that the righteous want above all to do God's will, so such petitions are heard.

What the light of the eyes means divides them. Gill takes it for the things seen rather than the power of seeing: gardens, rivers, meadows, hills and valleys, and above all light itself. Henry reads it so too and adds gratitude, since those who lack the mercy know its worth. Clarke turns it into a programme of study, nature and art setting resplendent images before a man with judgment and an accurate eye, who may instruct himself endlessly. Ellicott alone reverses direction: what does the heart good is seeing someone else whose eyes are bright with happiness. Delitzsch keeps to the lexicon and challenges a scholar who would emend the phrase, asking whether the noun really never means brightness but only a lamp.

The last verses turn on reproof and its refusal. Henry explains the phrase about the reproof of life two ways — such reproofs are given in a lively manner, by our lives as much as our doctrine, and they lead to life where taken — while Delitzsch confines the sense to instruction whose end is life, dismissing an emendation as a fancy. Ellicott notes that the ear stands for the person, Wesley that such a hearer seeks the company of the wise, Clarke that advice is for those who will take it. On the refuser, Delitzsch presses the Hebrew for soul, which means more than the later word for self, being the bond between intellectual and bodily life, so despising it is exposing one's life — in a word, suicide. Clarke gets there more cautiously, calling the self-hatred constructive rather than actual; Henry finds in it the sinner's fundamental error, an undervaluing of his own soul. The chapter closes on a proverb Delitzsch will not decide. The clause may be predicate, making the fear of God the aim of Wisdom's teaching, or subject, in which case the fear of God continually exercised is the right school of wisdom and humility the road to honour. Ellicott renders a discipline leading to wisdom. Clarke collects what the book has said of this fear — beginning of wisdom, beginning of knowledge, instruction of wisdom — and closes by observing that men who rose from low life to trust have been remarkable for humility, and that providence never elevates the proud.
